title: Interactions across hemispheres in prefrontal cortex reflect global cognitive processing

paper_content.abstract: Brain functions involve processing in local networks as well as modulation from brain-wide signals, such as arousal. Dissecting the contributions of populations of neurons to these functions requires knowledge of interactions between brain areas. We investigated these interactions using dual hemisphere recordings of prefrontal cortex in monkeys performing a spatial memory task. To tease apart global processing from local interactions, we applied a novel statistical approach called pCCA-FA (a combination of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis) to analyze trial-to-trial variability in neuronal activity. We found substantial shared variability among neurons within each population, much of which was actually shared across populations and linked to an arousal process. Our work presents a path by which we can leverage multi-area recordings to reveal aspects of brain functions that are hidden in single-area recordings.
paper_content.introduction:
Brain functions such as attention [1, 2], decision making [3], and working memory [4, 5] rely on coordination among neurons within brain areas as well as across brain areas. Thus, the spiking activity of individual neurons can be influenced by neurons from the same brain area, neurons in other brain areas, global modulatory signals, and more [6]. Teasing apart the impact of each of these influences on neural activity would enable a deeper understanding of how neurons in different brain areas interact to give rise to such brain functions.

To dissect the various influences on neural activity, we can consider how the activity of one neuron covaries with that of other nearby neurons. Many studies have examined how the activity of pairs of neurons in a single brain area covaries from trial-to-trial by computing spike count correlation (rsc) [7, 8]. These pairwise correlations have been widely used as a window to investigate a range of phenomena from cognitive states to circuit architectures [9, 10]. To go beyond pairs of neurons, a related body of work has identified the population-wide covariability structure in single brain areas. These population-level approaches have been used to study the trial-to-trial variability underlying sensory encoding [11, 12], attention [13, 14], motor control [15–17], learning [18–20], decision-making [21–23], network structure [24–26], and more [27]. Taken together, these studies inform our understanding of how neural activity is shared among neurons within a brain area.

Given that most brain functions rely on interactions across brain areas, it is likely that some component of the activity of each brain area is shaped by interactions with other brain areas. Developments in neural recording technology have enabled simultaneous recordings of populations of neurons in multiple brain areas [28–30], which give rise to the possibility of distinguishing interactions across brain areas from interactions solely within a single brain area [31–34]. Simultaneous recordings from multiple brain areas have been leveraged to study widespread brain functions such as sensory processing [35–40], motor control [41–44], learning [45–47], decision-making [50–52], working memory [48, 49], arousal [53, 54], and attention [55–60]. However, most statistical methods for analyzing populations of neurons are not designed to distinguish activity shared across areas from activity shared solely among neurons within each area.

Here, we seek to identify components of neural activity that involve interactions across two areas (i.e., an across-area component), as well as interactions solely within each area (i.e., a within-area component). We simultaneously recorded spiking activity from each of the two hemispheres (here referred to as two areas) of prefrontal cortex (PFC) in macaque monkeys while they performed a spatial memory task. Utilizing a statistical method we developed called pCCA-FA (a combination of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis), we found substantial shared variance among neurons in PFC, much of which involved neurons across both areas. In fact, the across-area component of PFC activity was larger than the within-area component. We then uncovered a link between the across-area component and a brainwide arousal process. Our work motivates a reinterpretation of shared variance among neurons within a brain area as arising from multiple sources, both within that area as well as via interactions across the brain.
paper_content.results:
To support perception, cognition, and action, each neuron’s activity can be shared with other neurons in the same brain area, as well as with neurons in other brain areas. Consider the spiking activity of two distinct populations of neurons, recorded simultaneously from two brain areas (area 1 and area 2, Fig. 1a). For each neuron, we would like to identify which aspects of its activity are shared with neurons in the other area (pink arrow) and which aspects are shared exclusively with neurons in the same area (blue arrow). To understand how the activity of neuron 1 in area 1 is shared with other neurons (i.e., to quantify the relationships described by the pink and blue arrows in Fig. 1a), we would like to partition its trial-to-trial spike count variance into an across-area component (termed across-area variance; Fig. 1b, pink), a within-area component (termed within-area variance; Fig. 1b, blue), and a component independent to this neuron (termed independent variance; Fig. 1b, gray).

2.1 Mean spike count correlation does not adequately partition shared variance

We simultaneously recorded spiking activity from neurons in both hemispheres of dorsolateral PFC to understand how neural activity was shared either across or within areas (Fig. 2a). We began by characterizing the pairwise interactions among neurons within each area using rsc. The spike counts used to compute rsc were taken from a one-second window during the delay period of a memory-guided saccade task (Fig. 2b). Throughout this work, we combined trials across conditions after removing condition-specific means, and removed slow-timescale trends to avoid spurious correlations [61] (see Methods, Supplementary Fig. 1).

The mean rsc among pairs of recorded neurons in a brain area is commonly taken to indicate the strength of shared activity among neurons. We computed rsc for each pair of neurons within each area (Fig. 2c, left and middle, example session), then averaged over the pairs to obtain a within-area mean rsc per session (right PFC within-area mean rsc = 0.029, left PFC within-area mean rsc = 0.033, example session). In the majority of sessions, we found that within-area mean rsc values were positive (Fig. 2d, top and middle).

To understand how activity is shared across areas, one approach is to compute rsc between pairs of neurons across areas (i.e., one neuron in each area). Mean rsc decreases for pairs of neurons as the physical distance between the neurons increases [62–64], and has been shown to be smaller for pairs of neurons across versus within brain areas [65]. We observed an across-area mean rsc that was close to zero (Fig. 2c, right; Fig. 2d, bottom). This might be taken to suggest that neurons within areas interact more strongly than across areas (Fig. 2d; p = 1.0e−13, pooled across animals and brain areas; one-tailed t-test), and that there are little to no interactions across the hemispheres of PFC.

However, there are several limitations to mean rsc measurements. First, by averaging over all pairs of neurons (either across or within areas), we ignore the breadth of rsc distributions (Fig. 2c). For example, if there are pairs of neurons with strong positive correlations and also pairs with strong negative correlations, the mean rsc might be close to zero even though many neuron pairs exhibit strong correlations. One way to identify neuron pairs with strong positive and negative correlations is to consider the relative tuning preferences of the neurons [66–70]. Indeed, when we computed mean rsc among subsets of across-area neuron pairs with similar tuning (Fig. 2e, top) and opposite tuning (Fig. 2e, bottom), we found that similarly tuned pairs of neurons exhibited positive rsc (mean rsc = 0.019; p = 1.6e−10, pooled across animals; one-tailed t-test), whereas oppositely tuned pairs of neurons exhibited negative rsc (mean rsc = −0.013; p = 1.e−7, pooled across animals; one-tailed t-test). Second, the within-area mean rsc does not reveal whether the activity shared among neurons in an area is also shared with other areas. Rather, all co-fluctuations among neurons in a brain area are collapsed into the within-area mean rsc. As such, within-area mean rsc could reflect interactions with other areas and/or global neuromodulation. Third, mean rsc (either across- or within-area) is not designed to identify the many possible population-wide co-fluctuations among neurons. Several distinct changes in population-wide co-fluctuations can result in the same change in mean rsc [71, 72]. By collapsing all interactions in one metric, we are unable to separately characterize the many influences on neural activity. Here we desire to leverage the simultaneity of our dual PFC recordings to dissect the multiple population-wide influences on across- and within-area activity (as in Fig. 1b).

2.2 pCCA-FA partitions across- and within-area shared variance

To explicitly partition across- and within-area variance, we can leverage statistical methods that take into account all simultaneously-recorded neurons together. In a single brain area, we can identify population-wide co-fluctuation patterns using factor analysis (FA) or related methods [73]. While this provides a more detailed view of population-wide covariability than mean rsc [72], these methods do not reveal whether activity fluctuations are shared with other brain areas. When recording from two brain areas simultaneously, we can identify variance shared among neurons across areas by employing canonical correlation analysis (CCA) or related methods [31]. However, neither CCA nor its probabilistic variant, pCCA [74], are designed to also identify variance shared only among neurons within each area (see Methods). Given that none of the aforementioned methods are designed to partition variance into both across-area and within-area components, a new approach is needed.

To address this need, we developed a dimensionality reduction method for two simultaneously recorded brain areas called pCCA-FA (a combination of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis), which partitions the variance of each area’s activity into an across-area component, a within-area component, and a component independent to each neuron. pCCA-FA can be applied to any two populations of simultaneously recorded neurons, and here we focus on the case where each population is recorded in a distinct brain area (Fig. 3a, area 1 and area 2). We seek to identify latent variables that capture co-fluctuations among neurons across areas (Fig. 3a, z, pink), as well as latent variables specific to each area that capture co-fluctuations exclusively among neurons within each area (Fig. 3a, area 1: z1, light blue; area 2: z2, dark blue). In total, pCCA-FA identifies three sets of latent variables: one across-area set, and a separate within-area set for each area. Because the within-area latent variables are specific to each area, the number of within-area latent variables for each area need not be the same.

pCCA-FA approximates neural activity as a weighted sum of the across-area latent variables (Fig. 3b, pink) and the within-area latent variables (Fig. 3b, light and dark blue for areas 1 and 2, respectively). The co-fluctuation patterns comprise the weights, which are estimated from the neural activity and fixed across all trials. The values of the latent variables can vary from trial to trial. Each co-fluctuation pattern can be represented as a vector in a population activity space, where each coordinate axis represents the activity of one neuron (Fig. 3c). Whereas the across-area co-fluctuation patterns are paired across areas (Fig. 3c, pink), the within-area co-fluctuation patterns are separate for each area (i.e., not paired across areas) (Fig. 3c, light and dark blue for areas 1 and 2, respectively).

For each neuron, we can quantify the proportion of its spike count variance explained by each set of latent variables. pCCA-FA partitions each neuron’s variance into a component that is described by the across-area latent variables (Fig. 3d, pink) and a component that is described by that area’s within-area latent variables (Fig. 3d, light and dark blue for areas 1 and 2, respectively). The residual variance not accounted for by across- or within-area latent variables is independent to each neuron (Fig. 3d, gray). Thus, pCCA-FA explicitly partitions the spike count variance of each neuron into across-area, within-area, and independent components (as in Fig. 1b).

To summarize the outputs of pCCA-FA, we define the following two metrics. First, to understand the extent to which a particular set of latent variables explains a neuron’s spike count variance, we define the across- and within-area percentage of variance shared among neurons (%sv). The values of this metric reflect the relative sizes of the bars in Fig. 3d. Across-area %sv is defined as the proportion of spike count variance explained by the across-area latent variables, averaged across neurons in each brain area (see Equation (8)). Within-area %sv is defined analogously using the within-area latent variables (see Equation (9)). Thus, each brain area has both an across-area %sv and a within-area %sv. Second, we quantify the complexity of the interactions described by each set of latent variables by computing its shared dimensionality (dshared) [25, 75]. A larger dshared would indicate more complex interactions among neurons, whereas a smaller dshared would indicate less complex interactions among neurons. Across- and within-area dshared are defined as the number of latent variables required to explain the across- or within-area variance, respectively (see Methods).

Before applying pCCA-FA to neural recordings, we performed extensive model validation. We verified that pCCA-FA accurately identified the ground truth %sv and dshared using simulated data with properties chosen to be similar to our neural recordings (Supplementary Figs. 2-3). We also found that pCCA-FA required fewer trials to recover the ground truth %sv and dshared than pCCA (Fig. 3e-f) because pCCA-FA has fewer parameters than pCCA (Supplementary Fig. 4). Further, pCCA-FA outperformed other dimensionality reduction techniques (pCCA and FA) on neural recordings (Supplementary Fig. 4). Thus, the pCCA-FA framework successfully captures how neurons in two brain areas covary by partitioning variance into across- and within-area components.

2.3 Across-area interactions were substantial and often greater than within-area interactions

To identify across- and within-area variance in our PFC recordings, we fit pCCA-FA to the same neural activity (with the same preprocessing) as in the rsc analyses (Fig. 2). For each session, pCCA-FA estimated a single set of across-area latent variables common to both areas and a separate set of within-area latent variables for each area. From the mean rsc values in Fig. 2, one might expect to uncover a large within-area component and small across-area component using pCCA-FA.

To determine if this was the case, we computed across- and within-area %sv and dshared. For the same example session as in Fig. 2c, we found that a substantial portion of variance was shared across areas (14.97% and 17.47%, for right and left PFC, respectively), compared to the variance shared exclusively within each area (5.65% and 7.47%, for right and left PFC, respectively) (Fig. 4a). This trend was evident across sessions, with the across-area %sv being larger than the within-area %sv (Fig. 4b; p = 2.6e−7, pooled across animals and brain areas; paired one-tailed t-test; see Supplementary Fig. 5 for a shuffle control). Thus, substantial across-area interactions were present in the PFC activity and identified by pCCA-FA (see also Supplementary Fig. 1e for the across-area correlation values computed using pCCA-FA), contrary to the intuition from measuring pairwise across-area rsc. This discrepancy can be understood by considering the sign of pairwise correlations among neurons (Fig. 2e, see Math Note A of ref. [72]). Mean rsc averages over positive and negative correlations found in individual pairs of neurons, whereas %sv accounts for both positive and negative correlations among neurons. Note that the values of across- and within-area %sv (like mean rsc) can depend on neuronal properties, including their physical distance and tuning preferences.

Having found that neurons tended to more strongly covary across areas than within each area, we next considered the complexity of these interactions. We found that the across-area dshared was also larger than the within-area dshared (Fig. 4c; p = 3.1e−6, pooled across animals and brain areas; paired one-tailed t-test). This indicated that, in addition to being stronger, the interactions we identified across areas were more complex than the interactions within each area. We further note that these findings are not a consequence of statistical bias in measuring across- versus within-area %sv and dshared (Supplementary Fig. 2).

2.4 Across- and within-area components involved different co-fluctuation patterns

We next sought to understand the population-wide co-fluctuation patterns represented by each set of latent variables, as they provide insight into the nature of the co-fluctuations among neurons (Fig. 5a). There are many possible population-wide co-fluctuations. Perhaps the simplest example is all neurons sharing the same-signed loading onto a latent variable, such that the population would all increase their activity together or decrease their activity together. We examined whether this was the case in our PFC recordings. For this analysis, we focused on the first co-fluctuation pattern of each ordered set, as it reflected a large proportion of the across- or within-area variance (Supplementary Fig. 6). We found that all neurons increasing their activity together or decreasing their activity together was not consistent with the across- or within-area co-fluctuation patterns we identified (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. 7).

We next asked whether across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns were similar to each other by computing the angle between them in population activity space (θestimated; Fig. 5a). They might be similar if two different processes (one global and one local) had a similar effect among the neurons. Alternatively, each process might engage distinct circuit mechanisms, yielding different co-fluctuation patterns. In an example session, we found that the across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns appeared visually distinct, and produced a θestimated of 72◦ (Fig. 5b). In all sessions, we found that the across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns had large θestimated (Fig. 5c), often close to 90◦, which would indicate distinct co-fluctuation patterns.

To further assess the extent to which the measured θestimated reflected true differences in the across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns, we created a simulation in which we defined the ground truth angle between across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns (θsim, see Methods, Supplementary Fig. 3). We simulated activity in each area with a specified value of θsim that was otherwise matched to the neural recordings in terms of the number of neurons, latent variables, and trials (see Methods). We found that, for any given θsim, the resulting distributions of θestimated (Fig. 5d, top) were narrower than what we observed in the neural recordings (Fig. 5c). Instead, if we sampled a different value of θsim for each simulated dataset uniformly from 45◦ to 90◦, we recovered a distribution of θestimated (Fig. 5d, bottom) that was similar to that observed in the neural recordings (p = 0.40, pooled across animals and brain areas; paired two-tailed t-test). We confirmed that the observed variation in θestimated from session to session was not related to the number of neurons or trials recorded (Supplementary Fig. 8). Furthermore, we determined that the variation in θestimated did not arise solely from sampling different subsets of neurons from session to session, although it still likely contributed (Supplementary Fig. 9). Together, these results indicate that across- and within-area components involved different co-fluctuation patterns that varied in their similarity from session to session.

2.5 Across-area latent variables were related to pupil diameter

Given that we found substantial across-area variance (Fig. 4) involving different co-fluctuation patterns than the within-area component (Fig. 5), we considered whether the across-area variance might be related to a brainwide process. Arousal is known to modulate activity of neurons throughout the brain [53, 54, 76–78]. In addition, arousal state has been linked to changes in both the tonic diameter of the pupil [79, 80] and event-related changes in pupil diameter [81, 82]. Changes in pupil diameter have also been linked to arousal-related changes in neural activity in both cortical [83–86] and subcortical [79, 87–89] regions. Given that arousal has been found to be a brainwide phenomenon, we wondered if it was related to the across-area variance we observed. Recall that the across-area component is defined as variance that is shared with one or more neurons in the other area (regardless of whether that variance is also shared with neurons in the same area). We therefore asked how well the across- and within-area latent variables identified by pCCA-FA explained variance in the pupil diameter (Fig. 6a).

To address this question, we measured the trial-by-trial pupil diameter during the delay period and adjusted the pupil diameter values to remove slow fluctuations in an analogous manner to the neural activity, yielding one pupil diameter measure per trial (see Methods, Supplementary Fig. 10a-b). We used the across- or within-area latent variables identified by pCCA-FA (i.e., either d across-area latent variables or dm within-area latent variables for area m; see Methods) to compute a trial-by-trial regression of the pupil diameter for each set of latent variables (Fig. 6b). Across sessions, we found that the across-area latent variables explained substantially more variance in the pupil diameter (mean r2 = 0.25) than the within-area latent variables (right PFC, mean r2 = 0.038; left PFC mean r2 = 0.030) (Fig. 6c; p = 1.3e−30, pooled across animals and brain areas; one-tailed t-test). Furthermore, we found that the across-area latent variables explained variance in the event-related changes in pupil diameter observed just after target onset (Supplementary Fig. 10; p = 1.1e−5, pooled across animals and brain areas; one-tailed t-test). Thus, the across-area latent variables may be related to multiple aspects of pupil-linked arousal. Taken together, these results are consistent with a link between the coordinated activity across brain areas and global cognitive processes such as arousal.
paper_content.methods:
4.1 Animal model
Three male rhesus macaque monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were used in this study. One animal was sourced from Tulane National Primate Research Center (Monkey Wa) and two animals were from Covance (Monkey Pe and Monkey Sa). They were 10 (Monkey Pe), 7 (Monkey Wa), and 7 (Monkey Sa) years old at the time of data collection. All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh, and were in accordance with the United States National Research Council’s Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

4.2 Surgical preparation
Each animal was surgically implanted with a titanium headpost, which was fixed onto the skull using titanium screws. This was necessary to limit head movement such that the position of the eyes could be tracked and neural activity recorded. Animals were then each implanted with two 96-electrode “Utah” arrays (Blackrock Neurotech, Salt Lake City, UT). Electrode arrays were placed on the prearcuate gyrus just anterior to the arcuate sulcus, one in each hemisphere. Surgeries were performed in sterile conditions under general anesthesia using isoflurane.

4.3 Electrophysiological methods
Animals were positioned 36 cm from a 21” cathode ray tube monitor with 1024x768-pixel resolution and a refresh rate of 100 Hz. Task stimuli were generated using custom-designed software in Matlab (Mathworks, Natick, MA) that utilized the Psychophysics toolbox extensions [139–141]. Signals from the implanted electrodes were band-pass filtered (0.3 - 7500 Hz) and then digitized at 30,000 Hz. For each electrode, spiking waveforms were defined as a 52-sample (1.73 ms) window of the filtered voltage signal triggered by the signal crossing a predefined threshold, and stored for offline analysis. The threshold was defined as a multiple of the root-mean-square voltage of a brief epoch of the raw signal on each electrode collected at the beginning of each session. All behavioral data and neural activity were recorded using a Grapevine recording system (Ripple, Salt Lake City, UT) for further offline processing and analysis.

4.4 Behavioral task
Animals were trained to perform a standard memory-guided saccade task [142]. At the beginning of each trial, a 0.5 degree diameter blue fixation circle appeared at the center of a gray screen. The animal initiated fixation within an invisible window (Monkey Pe: 2.4, Monkey Wa: 1.8, Monkey Sa: 2.9 degrees radius) centered on the fixation circle and then 200 ms later a white target flashed in the animal’s periphery (Monkey Pe: 11.8 or 17.5 degrees from fixation depending on the session, Monkey Wa: 11.6 degrees from fixation, Monkey Sa: a single value in the range of 8.0 - 15.6 degrees from fixation depending on the session, with one session containing multiple randomly interleaved distances in this range) at one of 4, 8, or 16 locations depending on the session. The white target remained on the screen for either 100, 200, or 400 ms (depending on the session) after which it was removed from the screen. The animal maintained fixation for a delay period drawn randomly from a uniform distribution between 1.5 and 3 seconds. After the delay, the fixation circle disappeared, which served as the go cue for the animal to initiate a saccade toward the remembered location where the white target flash had appeared. The animal had 500 ms (Monkey Sa: 400 ms) to initiate a saccade, and an additional 200 ms to reach the target location. Successful completion of a saccade was defined by the animal maintaining fixation within an invisible window (Monkey Pe: 4.1, Monkey Wa: 5.9 or 7.0, Monkey Sa: 4.1 degrees radius) centered at the target location for at least 100 ms. A liquid reward was delivered for a saccade to the correct location. For a subset of sessions, a dim white circle was flashed at the target location after saccade initiation to assist the animal in target acquisition. Trials were pseudo-randomized in blocks during which the animal was required to correctly complete all target directions before beginning a new block. In total, we collected 42 sessions of data (16 in Monkey Pe, 10 in Monkey Wa, and 16 in Monkey Sa). For each session, we considered only trials in which the animal successfully acquired the saccade target (i.e., correct trials). The number of correct trials per session for Monkey Pe was 729.8 ± 173.4 (mean ± standard deviation), for Monkey Wa was 463.5 ± 170.1, and for Monkey Sa was 850.1 ± 284.2.

4.5 Preprocessing of neural activity
We used a previously trained and published neural network to classify waveforms as spikes or noise [143]. Briefly, the network was trained on human-sorted waveforms to distinguish between waveforms putatively of neural origin and waveforms not of neural origin. Using this network, we removed threshold crossings that were unlikely to be of neural origin, and refer to the remaining waveforms as spikes. The spikes from each electrode on the Utah array were treated as multi-unit activity, and no further differentiation of single units was performed. Thus, each electrode was treated as one neural unit. Using multi-unit activity tends to yield higher correlation values than single unit activity [8], and this applies equally to the across-area and within-area measurements.

We removed electrodes that had very low firing rates or very high trial-to-trial variability. To do this, we first binned neural activity by counting spikes during the target presentation and delay period between target onset and saccade initiation cue. We then removed electrodes with mean spike count lower than 2 spikes/second or Fano factor greater than 10 during this time window. This served to eliminate electrodes contaminated by recording artifacts, or units that were not present for the entirety of a recording session. We also removed electrodes affected by artifactual cross-talk due to electrical coupling. For each pair of electrodes, we flagged spikes as coincident if they occurred within 100 µs of each other. If either electrode in the pair had 20% or more of its spikes flagged as coincident, we flagged that pair as having artifactual crosstalk. This procedure provided an index for each electrode of how many other electrodes it was coincident with. We then iteratively removed the electrode coincident with the highest number of other electrodes until no crosstalk remained, which ensured that the fewest possible number of electrodes were removed. After this process the number of remaining electrodes in Monkey Pe was 78.3 ± 7.8 and 79.5 ± 8.5 (mean ± standard deviation), in Monkey Wa was 85.3 ± 8.1 and 25.2 ± 4.4, and in Monkey Sa was 62.6 ± 9.8 and 75.3 ± 13.2 for right and left PFC respectively.

After the above preprocessing steps, the spiking activity was binned into spike counts. The bin was defined as the one second of the delay period immediately preceding the earliest possible saccade initiation cue in the session, such that each trial contributed one bin. For example, if the earliest possible saccade initiation cue in a given session was 1.5s after the target disappeared, the bin would be defined as 0.5-1.5s after the target disappeared for every trial in that session. This one-second window aggregated the interactions across and within brain areas observed during the delay period on the trial-to-trial timescale.

4.6 Computing signal correlation
In Fig. 2e, we investigated if the distribution of across-area rsc, despite having a mean near zero, contained pairs of neurons with positive rsc and other pairs of neurons with negative rsc, in a way that was systematically related to the neurons’ task tuning. To do this, we identified each neuron’s tuning across all of the saccade target locations. We determined whether each pair of neurons had similar or opposite tuning by computing their signal correlation. This was defined as the Pearson correlation between the two neurons’ raw trial-averaged responses to each of the possible targets (4, 8, or 16 depending on the session) during the one-second window described above. To assess significance for each neuron pair, we generated a chance distribution of correlation values by using a permutation test (shuffling the target location labels). We then labeled a neuron pair as having significant signal correlation (positive for similarly tuned and negative for oppositely tuned pairs) if their signal correlation was more extreme than the 99th percentile of the chance distribution. Neuron pairs not meeting this criterion were excluded from this analysis.

4.7 Combining trials across conditions
To increase the number of observations for model fitting, we combined trials across conditions (saccade target direction). To focus our analyses on trial-to-trial variability, for each neuron, we first subtracted the condition mean from the binned spike counts in each condition and then combined residual spike counts across conditions. Because the spike count variance can differ across conditions, the residual spike counts can still contain a small amount of condition-specific signal. An alternative approach is to z-score the spike counts for each neuron and condition before combining across conditions [63]. We repeated the key analyses related to the identification of shared variance among neurons in Figs. 2 and 4 using condition-specific z-scoring and found qualitatively similar results. Note, the computation of signal correlation (above) was performed before the subtraction of condition-specific means.

4.8 Separation of slow and fast components
In this work, we were interested in trial-to-trial variability of neural activity on a timescale of seconds. As we investigated interactions between left and right PFC, it soon became apparent that both areas also contained a component that varied slowly on a timescale of minutes to hours. While slow-timescale variability presents its own set of scientific questions (e.g., ref. [54]), these fluctuations complicated our analyses by introducing dependencies between one trial and the next, violating the basic independence assumption of correlation analysis (including regression, Pearson correlation, pCCA, and pCCA-FA). Therefore, we removed the slow component from the neural activity (see Supplementary Fig. 1), and focused all analyses in this work on faster-timescale trial-to-trial variability, except where noted in Supplementary Fig. 1 and for computing signal correlation. We computed the slow component for each session using a centered boxcar filter of length 25 trials, computed for each remaining electrode after the preprocessing described above. We then subtracted this component from the residual spike counts to remove slow-timescale trends that could have induced spurious correlations [61]. We performed this preprocessing procedure independently for each neuron. All analyses in this study were performed on the residual faster-timescale component, except where noted.

4.9 Preprocessing of pupil diameter
Eye position and pupil diameter were monitored using monocular infrared tracking at a 1000 Hz sample rate (EyeLink 1000, SR Research, Mississauga, Canada). On each trial, we measured the pupil diameter during the delay period, from target offset until the saccade initiation cue. Each trial was smoothed using a median filter with a 50ms window (i.e., the median value in a 50ms centered window was subtracted from each sample) to remove high frequency noise.

For the analyses in Fig. 6, we computed mean smoothed pupil diameter (arbitrary units) over the full time window described above to obtain the most robust estimate of the pupil diameter on each trial. This yielded one average pupil diameter value per trial. Like the preprocessing of neural activity, we removed slow-timescale fluctuations in pupil diameter using a centered boxcar filter of length 25 trials. This yielded what we termed the trial-by-trial pupil diameter (Supplementary Fig. 10a-b).

To ensure pupil data quality, we computed the variance across trials of the trial-by-trial pupil diameter. We then removed outlier sessions that exceeded a variance threshold of two times the interquartile range of the variance values across sessions. This was performed for each animal individually. This procedure excluded one session from Monkey Wa from analyses of the pupil (Fig. 6, Supplementary Fig. 10), resulting in n = 9 sessions for analysis. To ensure pupil diameter was on a similar scale across sessions, we z-scored the trial-by-trial pupil diameter for each session by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation across trials in the session.

4.10 Probabilistic canonical correlation analysis (pCCA)
A commonly used approach for identifying interactions between brain areas is canonical correlation analysis (CCA) [31]. Briefly, CCA attempts to find a co-fluctuation pattern in area 1 and a co-fluctuation pattern in area 2, such that neural activity along these co-fluctuation patterns is maximally correlated across areas. Further co-fluctuation patterns can be found subject to the constraint that they are uncorrelated with previous co-fluctuation patterns. The correlations along these co-fluctuation patterns are known as canonical correlations (ρ). Note that CCA identifies activity shared across areas, but is not designed to partition activity into across- and within-area components.

The probabilistic interpretation of CCA (pCCA [74]) is defined by the following model. pCCA defines a linear-Gaussian relationship between the spike count vectors x1 ∈ Rn1 from area 1 and x2 ∈ Rn2 from area 2 and the across-area latent variables z ∈ Rd as:

z ∼ N(0, Id)
x1 | z ∼ N(µ1 + W1z, Ψ1)
x2 | z ∼ N(µ2 + W2z, Ψ2) (1)

where n1 and n2 are the number of neurons recorded in areas 1 and 2, respectively, and d is the number of across-area latent variables. The identity matrix Id ∈ Rd×d describes prior covariance of the latent variables. The vectors µ1 ∈ Rn1 and µ2 ∈ Rn2 represent the mean spike counts of areas 1 and 2, respectively. The loading matrices W1 ∈ Rn1×d and W2 ∈ Rn2×d map the latent variables onto neural activity in areas 1 and 2 respectively, and Ψ1 ∈ Rn1×n1 and Ψ2 ∈ Rn2×n2 are full covariance matrices.

From Equation (1), the marginal distributions for x1 and x2 are:

x1 ∼ N(µ1, W1W1T + Ψ1)
x2 ∼ N(µ2, W2W2T + Ψ2) (2)

We can see that pCCA decomposes the covariance of neural activity from each area into a low-rank component shared across areas (e.g., W1W1T) and a full noise covariance matrix (e.g., Ψ1). Note that pCCA treats all variance which cannot be explained by across-area latent variables (z), including within-area interactions and variance independent to each neuron, as noise.

It can be shown that pCCA (Equation (1)) finds the same co-fluctuation patterns (described by W1 and W2) as CCA that maximize correlation across areas [74]. CCA and pCCA therefore identify the same canonical correlations.

4.11 Probabilistic canonical correlation analysis - factor analysis (pCCA-FA)
We developed a model called pCCA-FA (a combination of probabilistic canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis (FA [144])), which explicitly partitions covariance of neural activity into an across-area component, a within-area component, and a component independent to each neuron. Though we term the components across-area and within-area, the pCCA-FA framework can be applied to any two simultaneously-recorded populations of neurons. pCCA-FA is related to extensions of FA that have been proposed in other contexts, such as refs. [145] and [146].

pCCA-FA defines the linear-Gaussian relationship between the spike count vectors x1 ∈ Rn1 from area 1 and x2 ∈ Rn2 from area 2 and across-area latent variables z ∈ Rd and within-area latent variables z1 ∈ Rd1 and z2 ∈ Rd2 as:

z ∼ N(0, Id) z1 ∼ N(0, Id1) z2 ∼ N(0, Id2)
x1 | z, z1 ∼ N(µ1 + W1z + L1z1, Ψ1)
x2 | z, z2 ∼ N(µ2 + W2z + L2z2, Ψ2) (3)

where d is the number of across-area latent variables, and d1 and d2 are the number of within-area latent variables for areas 1 and 2, respectively. The identity matrices Id ∈ Rd×d, Id1 ∈ Rd1×d1, and Id2 ∈ Rd2×d2 describe the prior covariance of each set of latent variables. Given n1 neurons from area 1, W1 ∈ Rn1×d is the loading matrix for the across-area component in area 1, and L1 ∈ Rn1×d1 is the loading matrix for the within-area component in area 1. The matrix Ψ1 ∈ Rn1×n1 is a diagonal matrix containing the independent variance of each neuron in area 1, and µ1 ∈ Rn1 represents the mean spike counts of area 1. The parameters for area 2 are defined analogously.

From Equation (3), the marginal distributions for x1 and x2 are:

x1 ∼ N(µ1, W1W1T + L1L1T + Ψ1)
x2 ∼ N(µ2, W2W2T + L2L2T + Ψ2) (4)

We can observe that pCCA-FA decomposes the covariance of neural activity in area 1 as the sum of an across-area component (W1W1T), a within-area component (L1L1T), and an independent neuron component (Ψ1). The covariance of neural activity in area 2 is decomposed into analogous across-area (W2W2T), within-area (L2L2T), and independent neuron (Ψ2) components. In the pCCA-FA model, variance shared with neurons in the other area is assigned to the across-area component (appearing in the pCCA-FA model as Wm for each area m, and corresponding to latent variable z, which involves both areas), regardless of whether that variance is also shared with neurons in the same area. Consequently, variance is assigned to the within-area component only when it is not shared with any neuron in the other area (appearing in the pCCA-FA model as Lm, and corresponding to latent variable zm, which only involves area m).

pCCA-FA can be viewed as a combination of two existing latent variable methods, namely pCCA, which finds co-fluctuation patterns that maximize correlation between two populations, and FA, which maximizes covariance between neurons within a single population. Importantly, pCCA-FA explicitly identifies both types of covariance in a single probabilistic framework. The key difference between pCCA-FA and pCCA is that pCCA-FA constrains the full covariance matrices identified by pCCA (e.g., Ψ1 in Equation (2)) as low-rank plus diagonal (e.g., L1L1T + Ψ1 in Equation (4), see Supplementary Fig. 4). It follows that pCCA-FA has fewer parameters than pCCA, and is thus more robust in the regime of low trial counts (i.e., able to recover ground truth with fewer trials; Fig. 3e-f). With sufficient trials, pCCA-FA and pCCA identify the same across-area co-fluctuation patterns.

4.12 Fitting pCCA-FA
To fit pCCA-FA to neural activity, we define a joint vector of neural activity in both areas (x˜) and a joint vector of across- and within-area latent variables (˜z):

x˜ := [x1; x2] ˜z := [z; z1; z2]

The probabilistic model of pCCA-FA from Equation (3) can be rewritten as:

˜z ∼ N(0, Id+d1+d2)
x˜ | ˜z ∼ N(µ˜ + L˜˜z, Ψ˜) (5)

where

µ˜ = [µ1; µ2] L˜ = [W1 L1 0; W2 0 L2] Ψ˜ = [Ψ1 0; 0 Ψ2]

and µ1, µ2, W1, W2, L1, L2, Ψ1, and Ψ2 are defined as in Equation (3). The formulation in Equation (5) makes clear how we can think of pCCA-FA as a constrained and structured FA model. The zeros in the loading matrix L˜ ensure that the within-area latent variables (z1 and z2) are only used to explain activity in their respective areas, whereas across-area latent variables (z) are used to explain activity in both areas.

Based on Equation (5), the marginal distribution of the activity in both areas is:

x˜ ∼ N(µ˜, L˜L˜T + Ψ˜) (6)

We fit pCCA-FA model parameters to neural activity using an exact expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm [147]. The EM algorithm for pCCA-FA resembles that used for FA. Specifically, the M-step update equations for the parameters L˜ and Ψ˜ mirror those derived in FA for the loading matrix and noise covariance matrix. Each M-step parameter update for pCCA-FA (i.e., for parameters W1, L1, etc.) effectively applies a zeroing mask to the contents of L˜, ensuring that the blocked structure of the loading matrix is maintained. Additionally, there is no constraint on the relationship between the across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns (e.g., they are not constrained to be orthogonal).

The columns of each loading matrix (Wm and Lm for each area m) as estimated using the EM algorithm are not ordered. As a post-processing step for all analyses, we applied the singular value decomposition to transform each loading matrix, such that the first column contained the co-fluctuation pattern that explained the most shared variance, the second column explained the second-most shared variance, etc. For across-area co-fluctuation patterns, it may also be desirable to order the columns according to shared correlation (as in CCA, see below).

For each session, we jointly chose the dimensionalities for across- (d) and within-area (d1 and d2) latent variables using 10-fold cross-validation and selected the dimensionalities which maximized the cross-validated data likelihood P(x˜) (see Equation (6)). We tested integer dimensionality values between 1 and 15, inclusive, for both across- and within-area latent variables for each cross-validation run. After across- and within-area dimensionalities were selected, a final pCCA-FA model was fit with the specified dimensionalities using all trials. The parameters of this final model were used in all analyses.

4.13 Estimating latent variables in pCCA-FA
To estimate the across- and within-area latent variables in pCCA-FA (e.g., for use in predicting pupil diameter in Fig. 6), we computed the posterior mean of latent variables:

E[˜z | x˜] = L˜T (L˜L˜T + Ψ˜)−1 (x˜ − µ˜) (7)

where the first d entries of E[˜z | x˜] are E[z | x1, x2] (across-area latent variables), the next d1 entries are E[z1 | x1] (within-area latent variables for area 1), and the final d2 entries are E[z2 | x2] (within-area latent variables for area 2).

4.14 Computation of canonical variables
The pCCA-FA parameters allow for the computation of the canonical variables analogous to those found for CCA (Supplementary Fig. 6a). Following ref. [74], the canonical directions and correlations can be obtained applying the singular value decomposition on the cross-correlation matrix K ∈ Rn×n:

K = Σ11−1/2 Σ12 Σ22−1/2

where n is the total number of neurons (i.e., n1 + n2),

Σ11 = W1W1T + L1L1T + Ψ1
Σ22 = W2W2T + L2L2T + Ψ2
Σ12 = W1W2T

are the blockwise entries of L˜L˜T + Ψ˜. The canonical pairs of directions (u1i ∈ Rn1, u2i ∈ Rn2) for i = 1, 2, ..., d, are defined as:

(u1i, u2i) = (Σ11−1/2v1i, Σ22−1/2v2i),

where (v1i ∈ Rn1, v2i ∈ Rn2) are a pair of left-right singular vectors of K. The corresponding singular value ρi is the canonical correlation.

Note that the Σ matrices are defined in terms of the estimated pCCA-FA parameters rather than the sample covariance matrices (which is what CCA and pCCA use). This is the regularization that pCCA-FA provides that enables it to perform well in a limited data regime (Fig. 3e-f).

4.15 Measuring %sv and dshared
We defined two metrics to summarize the outputs of pCCA-FA: the percentage of variance shared among neurons (%sv) and shared dimensionality (dshared), which were originally introduced for FA [25, 72] and adapted here for pCCA-FA.

4.15.1 %sv
We used %sv to measure the prominence of (i.e., the proportion of variance explained by) the across- or within-area components. For a given pCCA-FA model, there are four instances of %sv: an across-area and a within-area instance, for each of the two areas. The across-area %sv quantifies the percentage of each neuron’s variance that was explained by across-area latent variables (i.e., the percentage of each neuron’s activity that was shared with at least one other neuron in the other area). More specifically:

Across-area %sv for neuron k in area m = (wmk wmkT) / (wmk wmkT + lmk lmkT + ψmk)

where wmk is the kth row of the across-area loading matrix for area m, lmk is the kth row of the within-area loading matrix for area m, and ψmk is the independent variance for the kth neuron in area m (i.e., the kth entry of the diagonal of Ψm). The numerator represents the across-area variance for neuron k in area m, and the denominator represents the total variance for that neuron. In our analyses of %sv, we averaged over neurons in a brain area to obtain a single across-area %sv metric for each area.

Similarly, the within-area %sv quantifies the percentage of each neuron’s variance that was explained by within-area latent variables (i.e., the percentage of each neuron’s activity that was shared with at least one other neuron in the same area, but was not shared with any neurons in the other area). More specifically:

Within-area %sv for neuron k in area m = (lmk lmkT) / (wmk wmkT + lmk lmkT + ψmk)

4.15.2 dshared
We used the metric, dshared, to measure the complexity of across- and within-area interactions. For a given pCCA-FA model, there are four instances of dshared, an across-area and a within-area instance, for each of the two areas. Note that dshared measures the dimensionality of interactions shared among neurons and excludes activity related to each neuron’s independent variance. We measured dshared in an analogous way to ref. [25], but adapted for across- and within-area dimensionalities.

Briefly, the first step in measuring across-area dshared is to fit the loading matrices Wm with d* across-area latent variables, where d* is the number of latent variables that maximizes the cross-validated data likelihood. Across-area dshared is defined for each area m as the minimum number of latent variables needed to explain at least 95% of the across-area shared covariance in WmWmT, where dshared ≤ d*. A 95% threshold was used in order to focus on latent variables that explain a large amount of shared variance. Note that although there is a single set of d* across-area latent variables, it is possible to obtain a different value of across-area dshared for each area.

We analogously defined within-area dshared for each area using the procedure described above by replacing WmWmT with LmLmT.

4.16 Simulated data generation
To validate the pCCA-FA model (Fig. 3e-f), as well as generate chance distributions (Fig. 5d), we generated simulated data xm for each area m from the pCCA-FA model according to Equation (4). This involved defining ground truth model parameters µm, Wm, Lm, and Ψm for each area m.

For model validation in Fig. 3e-f, we defined these parameters in the following way. We generated random loading matrices Wm and Lm for each area m using independent draws from a standard normal distribution. We scaled the %sv in each loading matrix by adjusting the singular values of the across- and within-area loading matrices (Wm and Lm) relative to each other to achieve the desired ratios (≈ 15% across-area and ≈ 10% within-area). The independent variance values (i.e., entries of Ψm) were then scaled to achieve a level of 75%. Each simulated dataset had 30 neurons per area, 5 across-area latent variables (d = 5), and 3 within-area latent variables per area (dm = 3 for each area m). For each trial count configuration, we generated 30 sets of ground truth parameters and a single simulated dataset per set of parameters.

For Fig. 5d, we defined the ground truth model parameters to be copies of those that were estimated from each of the neural recordings, with one manipulation, described below. For the chance distributions in Fig. 5d and the simulated data in Supplementary Fig. 3, we specified the angle between across- and within-area co-fluctuation patterns (θsim). To achieve this, we held the across-area loading matrix (Wm) constant and set the first column of the within-area loading matrix (Lm) to be a vector that was θsim degrees apart from the first column of Wm. The remaining columns of the within-area loading matrix were randomly generated from a standard normal distribution, and then orthogonalized relative to the first column (i.e., the first column remained fixed and the remaining columns were set to be mutually orthogonal to it).

4.17 Fitting pCCA-FA and pCCA to simulated data
To fit pCCA-FA to simulated data for the analysis in Fig. 3e-f, we used the EM algorithm described above. Across- and within-area dimensionalities were estimated in a cross-validated manner. Candidate dimensionalities for across- and within-area ranged from 1 to 10 (inclusive), for both across- and within-area latent variables. After the across- and within-area dimensionalities were selected, a final pCCA-FA model was fit with the specified dimensionalities using all simulated trials. The parameters of this final model were used to compute %sv and dshared.

To fit pCCA, we used an analogous EM algorithm, presented in ref. [74]. We fit pCCA to the same sets of simulated data as pCCA-FA. The across-area dimensionality was estimated in a cross-validated manner. Candidate dimensionalities for the across-area latent variables ranged from 1 to 10 (inclusive). After the across-area dimensionality was selected, a final pCCA model was fit with the specified dimensionality using all simulated trials. The parameters of this final model were used to compute across-area %sv and dshared.

4.18 Pupil diameter regression
To explain pupil-related variance using the latent variables estimated by pCCA-FA, the across-area latent variables E[z | x1, x2] and the within-area latent variables E[z1 | x1] and E[z2 | x2] were estimated using Equation (7). We regressed either the across-area or the within-area (right or left PFC) latent variables onto the trial-by-trial pupil diameter using a linear regression model for each set of latent variables. We then assessed r2, the proportion of variance in the trial-by-trial pupil diameter explained by the regression model.

To compute chance distributions, we repeated the procedure above, except that we performed the regression using latent variables estimated from the neural activity from a different session than the one in which we measured pupil diameter (i.e., the latent variables from session i were used to explain variance in the pupil diameter from session j, where i ≠ j). Trials were truncated in the session with more trials to ensure equal trial numbers. Chance distributions contained 240 samples for Monkeys Pe and Sa with 16 sessions, and 72 samples for Monkey Wa with 9 sessions. We report the 95% confidence intervals of this chance distribution (Fig. 6c, gray bars, termed shuffle). An alternative method to generate the chance distribution involves performing a within-session shuffle, in which the latent variables from session i are used to explain variance in the pupil diameter from session i but with permuted trial labels. This procedure yielded a similar, but slightly more lenient, chance distribution.

To control for differences in the number of across- and within-area latent variables, we repeated the entire procedure using only one predictor (i.e., the top across- or within-area latent variable) rather than the full set of predictors (i.e., d across- or dm within-area latent variables). This yielded similar results (p = 4.3e−22; pooled across animals and brain areas, n = 82 brain areas, 2 per session; one-tailed t-test on the differences in r2 for each session).

4.19 Statistical tests and reproducibility
Data preprocessing was performed using custom code in MATLAB (Mathworks, Natick, MA). Criteria for inclusion of units are described in Methods section: Preprocessing of neural data. All analyses were performed in Python (version 3.8.18). Statistical tests (t-test) were performed using the SciPy (version 1.10.0, https://scipy.org) statistics module. Sample sizes and p-values are directly reported in the corresponding figure caption. Averaged data shown in figures are averaged across sessions (n=42) or brain areas (n=84, 2 per session), noted in each caption. For data shown in histograms, means are marked with triangles. Detailed descriptions of plotted data are provided in each caption. Code to reproduce the figures and statistics is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/meganmcd13/figures-dual-pfc.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper develops a method combining canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis and applies it to simultaneously recorded spike activity from both sides of the monkey's lateral prefrontal cortex during a delayed eye movement task, and decomposes the intertrial variability of the activity into a common component between the left and right prefrontal areas and a component within each area. By showing that the common inter-areal component corresponds well to the pupil diameter reflecting the arousal level, they demonstrated that this method can explain specific phenomena effectively.
Both canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis are major data analysis methods, but I appreciate the fact that this method integrates them in a straightforward manner to obtain previously unobtainable results. The description is also clear and easy to understand, and the validity of the method and results is well verified. Therefore, I have no major objections to the scientific significance of this paper, and I will limit myself to making a few not-so-serious points regarding the acceptance or rejection of this paper. However, I have added some comments at the end that are not related to the acceptance or rejection of the paper. I hope they will find them useful in their future research.
Major
・The limitations of this method have not been discussed. What is supposed to be assumed by this method? What kinds of things might be missed? It seems natural, in a sense, that left and right hemisphere activity would co-vary with arousal state, but why was this not seen in a simple correlation and could only be obtained with the present method? etc. These questions need to be answered.
・Canonical correlation analysis assumes that correlations exist. Will this method ever produce a pseudo correlation? In other words, will data from different trials or from different animals, measured under the same task conditions, produce any pseudo-positive results?
・Is it possible to interpret the significance of the dimensions obtained? If this question is wrong, there is no need to answer it.
Minor
・I suppose they have performed single-unit sorting. If my understanding is correct, describe it clearly.
・If rsc is calculated from multi-unit activity, will inter-regional correlations be obtained?
・Is it possible to interpret the significance of the dimensions obtained? If this question is wrong, there is no need to answer it.
・Schwartz and Goldman-Rakic's anatomical study [82] has indicated that nerve connections between the left and right prefrontal cortex are “comb-like.” The Utah array may also include areas that are directly innervated from the contralateral side and areas that are not. The correlations may then differ significantly depending on the electrodes in the Utah array.
・It would be helpful to the reader if the recovery of the %sv and dshared in Fig. A3 had a figure that clearly explains why this method requires less data than pCCA. If it is not easy to illustrate, it is not required.
Comments
This method is interesting as a data analysis method and has a wide range of applications. For example, it may be used to determine the extent to which fluctuations in U.S. and Japanese stock prices are due to bilateral and domestic factors, respectively. Of course, the method could be applied to LFP (local field potential) as well as to spike activity. I have no doubt about the usefulness of this method.
However, I did not find in this paper much willingness or a clear perspective to delve into the nature of how the brain interacts between the cerebral hemispheres.
If they wanted to examine interhemispheric interactions using the ODR task, they should have included an anti-saccade task or some other experimental paradigm that required specific information to be exchanged between the two hemispheres.
The bin width of 1 second does not seem appropriate either. The exchange of information between hemispheres necessary to accomplish a task should occur in a much shorter time span. I know that many neurons in the prefrontal cortex have low firing rates. If so, then the instantaneous firing rate or other similar index should be used.
What information is carried from the contralateral area and how is it carried? Is it carried in different rhythms depending on the situation or is there a specific time window? Does a variety of information arrive unselected or is it carefully chosen? Some diseases, such as patients with apraxia, have problems with the consistency of information processing between hemispheres. It is the mission of brain scientists to try to get to the essence of how functional differentiation and integration between hemispheres is achieved.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In their manuscript “Interactions across hemispheres in prefrontal cortex reflect global cognitive processing”, McDonnell et al. propose a method termed pCCA-FA (probabilistic canonical correlation analysis in combination with factor analysis) to study interactions within and between the left and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (also termed regions or areas here). For each neuron, pCCA-FA estimates the proportion of trial-by-trial spike count variance attributable to self, within-region, and across-region sources. The authors also apply SVD to extract the main latent variables underlying these sources. They show that this approach offers advantages over previous methods (rSC, pCCA, or FA). They applied this method to study the populations of each prefrontal cortex in rhesus monkeys trained on a memory-guided saccade task. They find that the primary latent variable representing the across-area co-fluctuation pattern is a more effective predictor of pupil diameter than the corresponding within-area latent variable. Since pupil diameter is a marker of arousal, a brain-wide process, this finding supports that pCCA-FA can find truthful and insightful patterns and sources of variability in the brain.
I thought the approach the authors propose to study neuronal interactions is elegant and simple. pCCA-FA combines two well-established methods and, as far as I understand, is solidly constructed. They also provide an adequate justification for the need for a novel analysis tool. However, aspects related to the application of the method to the dataset and the interpretation of the results could be further refined.
General points:
1. There is a discrepancy between the title and narrative of the manuscript. From the title, one would think that the main focus of the paper is the study of “global cognitive processing,” which is indeed addressed in Results section 2.5, where pupil diameter is analysed. However, the discussion recurrs only briefly to this topic. I would like to see more efforts to relate the findings to cognition or, alternatively, a change in the title.
2. It is unclear to me why both the “mean pupil diameter” and the “pupillary evoked response magnitude” are analysed. The differences between these two measurements, as well as their cognitive interpretation, are not discussed.
3. In the discussion, it is mentioned that anatomical constraints on network circuitry may affect the correlation between neurons [line 363]. However, the cited papers are about visual, not prefrontal cortex. I would sugges to include more appropriate references, e.g. Kritzer & Goldman-Rakic, 1995, Journal of Comparative Neurology; Pucak, Levitt, Lund, & Lewis, 1996, Journal of Comparative Neurology
4. The results for the two different eye-pupil measures appear to differ slightly, particularly for monkey “Wa.” Moreover, monkey “Wa” shows overall different values for rsc, %sv, and dshared. Is there any interpretation of these differences?
Particular points:
[103-105] The phrasing in this sentence could be clearer. Since coordination between neurons is defined as synchronized patterns of activity, describing it as a process that causes or “results” in such patterns may appear tautological. This could also unintentionally suggest that neurons coordinate through signals other than their activity. Rewording the sentence could help avoid this ambiguity.
[140] What statistical test was performed here? If I understood correctly, none of the tests shown in Fig. 2 directly compare the distributions of rSC within versus across regions.
Additionally, for monkey “Wa,” the distributions of average rSC within and across regions across all sessions do not appear very different to the naked eye.
[248-251] Is this discrepancy the only reason that rSC is smaller than %sv? Could it be resolved simply by taking the absolute value or the squared value (as is done with %sv)?
[316-317] The “pupillary evoked response magnitude” is measured “just after visual stimulus presentation,” which occurs before the delay period. From the current wording (“across-area latent variables were able to explain multiple aspects of pupil-linked arousal”), one might infer a causal role from the latent variable to the pupillary evoked response. However, the neuronal activity is recorded “1 second of the delay period immediately preceding the earliest possible saccade initiation cue in the session.” Therefore, it cannot be concluded that the “latent variables identified by pCCA-FA explained changes in pupil diameter,” since the change in pupil diameter precedes the neuronal activity, implying that the causal direction would be reversed.
[331-332] I would argue that this is not, in general, “the shared variance among PFC neurons.” Here, task conditions (right or left stimulus cue, or right or left response) are pooled together. Therefore, it specifically measures the task-condition-independent variance. This distinction is significant because the PFC is primarily involved in processes that are task-dependent, where the task condition plays an important role. Thus, the analysis is capturing the shared variance of a specific sub-process within the PFC.
[481-485] Why was the entire electrode signal removed instead of only removing the repeated units? Could this approach be removing nearby neurons that might be more connected, thereby further reducing the %sv of inter-region units?
[500-502] If I understand correctly, the intention of this procedure is to remove condition-specific rate properties. However, this method only removes cue-specific rate variations, omitting response-specific variations. In other words, when pooling both correct and incorrect trials, for the same cue condition, there can be two overlapping modes of firing rate depending on whether the response was right or left. The paper does not specify which trials were selected (all or only correct) or what the hit rate was.
Furthermore, it would strengthen the manuscript to demonstrate that condition-mean subtraction effectively removes condition-specific activity patterns. This could be done, for example, by training a model to classify trials by condition before and after rate manipulation, showing that condition-mean subtraction renders the conditions indistinguishable.
[503] It is mentioned that z-scoring “yielded qualitatively similar rSC results,” but nothing is said about its effect on the pCCA-FA results. Should we expect that z-scoring would also lead to similar outcomes in pCCA-FA as in rSC?
[818-827] Why was the null distribution of the regressions created by shuffling neuronal activity from neurons in other sessions? Why not simply shuffle the pupil diameter values within a session while using the firing rates of the same neuron but from other trials?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This is an interesting and important paper of potentially high impact describing a new statistical technique developed by the authors that can parse components of variation in population activity patterns attributable to local interactions between neurons and inputs from neurons in another brain area.
This is a key challenge in deciphering the computational organization of the cerebral cortex, and it is the advantage of this technique over alternative methods. The technique could significantly advance our understanding of the interplay between local processing in cortical areas and large scale communication in cortical networks.
Nearly all of the questions I initially had about the validity of the technique were answered by results provided in Extended data. Generally, I recommend promoting as many of the highlights of the Extended results into additional panels of the main figures as possible, so that the majority of the readership sees the strong evidence validating the new technique.
In addition to describing and validating a new analytical technique, the paper provides important new information about the coordination of neural activity in prefrontal cortex, including the findings that correlations between brain areas (left and right hemispheres) are stronger than correlations within areas, and that the strength of within and between area neural correlations track several behavioral variables.
Major
1. The paper could be strengthened by enhancing the presentation of the data validating the pCCA-FC technique. Much of the crucial information is provided in the Extended Data. This includes: (1) comparison of detected correlations in the original data with trial shuffled data (Fig. A1), (2) relation of noise correlation to signal correlation (Fig. A2), (3) recovery of ground truth parameters from simulated data (Fig. A3), and (4) evidence that the pCCA-FC technique outperforms alternative methods (FIg. A3). The paper could be strengthened if some of the key panels from these figures were promoted to the main figures of the paper (for example adding them to Fig. 3). This would strengthen the case that the analysis developed by the authors measures real neural correlations, successfully parses variation within and between cortical areas, and outperforms existing methods
2. Related to the above, trial shuffling is utilized in the extended data to validate removal of slow sources of correlation over trials (Fig. A1). The current data could be strengthened by showing that trial shuffling destroyed detected neural correlations at faster time scales after removal of the slower components of correlation. This would substantiate that detected neural correlations depended on the simultaneity of the neural signals and were not artifacts of the analysis. The amount of correlation detected in the trial shuffled data (in some cases ~10%, Fig. 1Ad) was not trivial in relation to the magnitude of the correlation in the original data (~10-15%, Fig. 4B). It would therefore be important to show that the neural correlations detected by this method significantly exceed the level of correlation seen after trial-shuffling.
3. A key claim/finding is that the new analysis can parse correlations driven by local interactions between neurons from correlations driven by input from other brain areas. If this is true, differences in %sv attributable to interactions within and between cortical areas should be greater in the original data than after shuffling neurons between brain areas (randomly changing right/left hemisphere labels). Demonstrating that with an additional bootstrap test if feasible would strengthen the main claim of the paper.
4. More %sv was attributed to interactions between than within brain areas. The models derived to estimate %sv between areas had more free parameters (a greater number of latent parameters). It will be important for the main findings of the paper to argue/show that the difference in %sv attributed to local and long tract interactions did not reflect differences in the number of latent parameters in the models used to fit the two types of interactions.
5. The analysis is built to detect noise correlations, e.g. correlations in neural signals after modulation of activity due to task performance has been subtracted out. Relations to behavior (pupil diameter, spatial tuning) are therefore indirect. Can the technique be adapted to detect correlations in neural signal (task-related modulations in firing rate)? This would enhance links between detected correlations and behavior. Some description of how this might be done in future studies in the Discussion could be useful to understand the potential applicability of the technique to different questions.
6. It would be useful to clarify the link between detected neural correlations and the physiological processes that are likely to generate them, namely synaptic interactions between neurons. In particular, how do the authors envision that synaptic interactions between neurons could drive correlations in firing rate at the trial level that are captured by their analysis? For example, correlations in delay period firing rate over trials could reflect net excitatory and inhibitory synaptic interactions between neurons integrated over the 1 sec delay period, etc.
7. Related to point 6 above, the authors hypothesize that inter-area correlation is driven by a global neuromodulatory signal (such as NE) potentially linked to arousal. If the signal is global, why would it preferentially strengthen correlations between neurons in different brain areas in comparison to correlations between neurons in the same area? The logic here needs additional clarification.
8. Also related to point 6 above, it is thought that more synapses onto cortical pyramidal neurons derive from neighboring neurons in the same brain area than from neurons in distant areas. If synapses from recurrent local circuits do in fact provide the bulk of synaptic input, why then do inputs from remote brain areas drive stronger correlations? It could be useful to consider the correlation results in the context of what is known about the architecture of local versus long-tract connections, and to reconcile apparent discrepancies between the relative strength of connections and the relative strength of correlations.
Minor
1. The Methods describe training a neural network to distinguish neural action potential waveforms from noise. Were action potential waveforms from different neurons discriminated? If not, it would be important to state that the analysis was conducted on multi-neuron firing rates.
2. The paper does an excellent job of introducing the statistical concepts behind the technique. Any additional walk-throughs of the main concepts that the authors can provide would be to the good, to clarify the relationship between the loading matrices, latent variables, and population activity vectors, and how they combine to generate the co-fluctuation in firing patterns illustrated schematically in Fig. 3b.

This paper develops a method combining canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis and applies it to simultaneously recorded spike activity from both sides of the monkey's lateral prefrontal cortex during a delayed eye movement task, and decomposes the intertrial variability of the activity into a common component between the left and right prefrontal areas and a component within each area. Both canonical correlation analysis and factor analysis are major data analysis methods, but I appreciate the fact that this method integrates them in a straightforward manner to obtain previously unobtainable results. The description is also clear and easy to understand, and the validity of the method and results is well verified. Therefore, I have no major objections to the scientific significance of this paper, and I will limit myself to making a few not-so-serious points regarding the acceptance or rejection of this paper. Major
The limitations of this method have not been discussed. What is supposed to be assumed by this method? What kinds of things might be missed? It seems natural, in a sense, that left and right hemisphere activity would co-vary with arousal state, but why was this not seen in a simple correlation and could only be obtained with the present method? etc. These questions need to be answered.
We thank the reviewer for these suggestions, we have reworked the Discussion in order to incorporate these answers.
First, for the assumptions and limitations of pCCA-FA:
1. Like other similar dimensionality reduction methods, pCCA-FA defines a linear-Gaussian relationship between the latent variables and the neural activity. We state this in the Methods section (L694), and we have now additionally brought this up as a potential extension of pCCA-FA in Discussion (L459).
2. pCCA-FA is designed to identify latent variables that capture variance that is shared among neurons. Each method has a different objective function of what the latent variables are intended to capture. For example, one can use a targeted dimensionality reduction approach to identify activity that covaries with stimulus or behavioral variables (dPCA, Kobak, et al. 2016). The extension of pCCA-FA to identify other types of variance is now brought up in Discussion (L456).
3. Limitations such as hyperparameter selection, run time, and other logistic concerns are now described more thoroughly in Discussion.
Second, for what could be missed:
1. Related to the above assumption that pCCA-FA is a linear method, we could miss out in identifying nonlinear interactions among neurons. We have now noted this as an extension of pCCA-FA in Discussion (L459).
2. pCCA-FA is a static method and, thus, does not incorporate the concept of time. pCCA-FA is designed to be applied to a single time bin of neural activity per trial (across many trials). Both of these limitations are not specific to pCCA-FA, but rather apply to the entire class of static linear-Gaussian dimensionality reduction techniques (including FA, pCCA, and principal component analysis). We have now noted this as an extension of pCCA-FA in Discussion (L452).
3. Variance assigned to the within-area component of neural activity could, in fact, be shared with a non-recorded brain area. Similar interpretational considerations are present for any dimensionality reduction method. We bring this point up in Discussion (L385).
Third, for why we could not uncover the connection to arousal using a simple correlation: A simple correlation measure (r ) was also able to uncover co-fluctuations across the hemispheres of PFC (Fig. 2). However, simple correlation does not isolate the interactions that are shared across hemispheres from those within hemispheres. By applying pCCA-FA, we specifically isolate the component of neural activity that is shared across hemispheres, and we found that this component (and not the within-area component) was related to arousal state (Fig. 6). As such, a simple correlation of neural activity to the pupil diameter would not have been as effective as our approach. We further discuss the limitations of mean r in Results section “Mean spike count correlation does not adequately partition shared variance”.

We agree with the reviewer that canonical correlation analysis and correlational methods as a whole are susceptible to pseudo-correlations. This motivated our preprocessing step of removing slow-timescale trends, as we illustrate in Supplementary Fig. 1. In Supplementary Fig. 1c, we show that it is indeed possible to uncover pseudo-correlations using pCCA-FA. This is not a drawback of pCCA-FA per se, but rather it applies to any correlational method.
